Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 3 Campaign (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 3 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-3/)
Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 4 Campaign (https://www.cafairelections.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 4 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-4/)
Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 5 Campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 5 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-5/)
Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 37 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-37/)
Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.

What is immunotherapy?

Where does the money from Prop 38 go?
Prop 38's innovative network funding model supports California's universities and nonprofit research institutions through equal parts direct funding and investments in new, shared research resources and facilities anchored at a nonprofit institution.
Half of the funds will go to a nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm). This world-class research center will bring together leading scientists, advanced technology, specialized laboratory facilities, patients and clinical trials to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures. This institute will be selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) based on strict accountability requirements.
The other half of funds will be awarded competitively through a grant program to leading universities and nonprofit research institutions across California. This will be overseen by an Advisory Council of leading scientists, doctors and researchers in the field of immunology.
Ultimately, Prop 38 is designed to create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines broad competitive funding with a world-class institution capable of accelerating discoveries into life-saving treatments for patients.

Myths vs Facts
Get the facts on Prop 38. Learn what the initiative will do and find answers to some of the most common questions about Prop 38.
Updated October 26, 2026
Can California afford Prop 38?
Fact: Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#accountability). 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go back to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), covering both the principal and the interest of the bonds. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most prevalent diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses for Californians by tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses and lower insurance premiums.
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits. Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on saving lives.
For the millions of families that are facing life-threatening and life-altering diseases that take away our loved ones, we can’t afford NOT to invest in promising cures .
Why does California need Prop 38 when the federal government funds medical research too?
Fact: Prop 38 responds to massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty that are shutting down life-saving medical research (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) at California universities and research institutes. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can’t afford to wait.
Prop 38 creates a stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts to accelerate the pace of discoveries to help the tens of millions of patients fighting cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other debilitating diseases.
Prop 38 will make California a national leader in breakthrough medical research , fostering collaboration between leading California-based universities, scientists and physicians.
Prop 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs . Scientific research has become a critical economic engine in California, and studies show (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf) that each dollar invested in medical research returns three dollars back into our state’s economy.
Does half of Prop 38 funding go to one research institute?
Fact: Half of Prop 38 funding will support a world-class nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California with access to leading scientists, technology, laboratory equipment, patients and clinical trials necessary to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.
The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy will very likely apply for funding and meet qualification requirements. However, state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific named institute (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-12/) but can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. Ultimately, the California Department of Public Health is charged with determining which institute receives the funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm).
Will scientists or politicians decide which research Prop 38 funds?
Fact: Under Prop 38, scientists and researchers oversee a competitive process to ensure the most qualified research with life-saving potential is awarded funding. Prop 38 establishes an Advisory and Accountability Research Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), composed of members from seven University of California campuses and 10 – 15 members from California nonprofit universities and academic and research institutions. Each member of the council will be a physician, scientist or researcher with demonstrated experience in the field of immunology and immunotherapy.
Should the private sector fund this research instead of Prop 38?
Fact: Public funding like Prop 38 is vital to support medical research. More than 99% of new FDA-approved drugs from 2010 to 2019 were built on publicly funded research. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2804378) Prop 38 builds on this proven model by supporting universities and nonprofit researchers to move discoveries from the lab to patients faster and more cost-effectively.
Will the people funding Prop 38 benefit financially?
Fact: Prop 38 is funded by a doctor and philanthropists who will not benefit financially. Only public universities and nonprofit research institutions in California are eligible to receive research funding.
YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocates (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses AssociationCalifornia, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson’s Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, as well as patients, doctors and researchers because it will accelerate life-saving cures. This is a publicly accountable, voter-approved bond.

01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.
Broad agreement. One conclusion.
A growing coalition says No on Proposition 38.
Across the political spectrum, respected editorial boards, civic organizations, progressive groups and taxpayer advocates agree: Proposition 38 is the wrong way to fund medical research.

Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

Read the Measure
Read Proposition 38’s complete text as published in California’s Official Voter Information Guide.
Read it yourself Note the highly specific eligibility criteria for the single institute that would receive half the bond funds—criteria CalMatters reported very likely exclude all but one recipient. Read the full measure ↗ (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)Official voter guide ↗ (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm)
01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.
Broad agreement. One conclusion.
A growing coalition says No on Proposition 38.
Across the political spectrum, respected editorial boards, civic organizations, progressive groups and taxpayer advocates agree: Proposition 38 is the wrong way to fund medical research.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 3 Campaign (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 3 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-3/)
Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 4 Campaign (https://www.cafairelections.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 4 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-4/)
Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 5 Campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 5 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-5/)
Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 37 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-37/)
Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
No on Prop 38 Campaign (https://votenoonprop38.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 38 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-38/)
Proposition 39
PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts. It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions to put it on the ballot.
California’s elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in person, and match every mail ballot signature.
A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a driver’s license or Social Security number.
Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name, address, and signature.
Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote again.
An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on them.
A modern-day poll tax. A “free” ID is not free. Getting one costs transportation, childcare, time off work, and fees for the paperwork behind it. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters with disabilities, and voters of color are hit hardest.
Valid ID still must match. Nearly 30 percent of U.S. adults have changed their name, 94 percent of them women. Californians who took a new name at marriage, and transgender voters whose documents lag may hold valid ID and be turned away anyway.
Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them from voter rolls.
Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay, and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to spread lies.
Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards, audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don’t let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
No on Prop 39 Campaign (https://noonprop39.com/)

Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.

Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.

Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.

Proposition 38 on the November ballot authorizes the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy.
But half of that money must go to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute based on criteria that has no bearing on the ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research.
...
It would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy to identify treatments and cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease.
...
The measure requires the California Department of Public Health to give half the bond money — $4.2 billion — to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute that meets a long and unusual list of criteria, including occupying a minimum 200,000-square-foot space and receiving a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
These requirements have no bearing on an institution’s ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research.
Instead, they’re written so that a lone research center is eligible to receive the lion’s share of taxpayer money: the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.

Myths vs Facts
Get the facts on Prop 38. Learn what the initiative will do and find answers to some of the most common questions about Prop 38.
Updated October 26, 2026
Can California afford Prop 38?
Fact: Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#accountability). 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go back to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), covering both the principal and the interest of the bonds. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most prevalent diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses for Californians by tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses and lower insurance premiums.
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits. Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on saving lives.
For the millions of families that are facing life-threatening and life-altering diseases that take away our loved ones, we can’t afford NOT to invest in promising cures .
Why does California need Prop 38 when the federal government funds medical research too?
Fact: Prop 38 responds to massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty that are shutting down life-saving medical research (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) at California universities and research institutes. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can’t afford to wait.
Prop 38 creates a stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts to accelerate the pace of discoveries to help the tens of millions of patients fighting cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other debilitating diseases.
Prop 38 will make California a national leader in breakthrough medical research , fostering collaboration between leading California-based universities, scientists and physicians.
Prop 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs . Scientific research has become a critical economic engine in California, and studies show (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf) that each dollar invested in medical research returns three dollars back into our state’s economy.
Does half of Prop 38 funding go to one research institute?
Fact: Half of Prop 38 funding will support a world-class nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California with access to leading scientists, technology, laboratory equipment, patients and clinical trials necessary to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.
The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy will very likely apply for funding and meet qualification requirements. However, state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific named institute (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-12/) but can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. Ultimately, the California Department of Public Health is charged with determining which institute receives the funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm).
Will scientists or politicians decide which research Prop 38 funds?
Fact: Under Prop 38, scientists and researchers oversee a competitive process to ensure the most qualified research with life-saving potential is awarded funding. Prop 38 establishes an Advisory and Accountability Research Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), composed of members from seven University of California campuses and 10 – 15 members from California nonprofit universities and academic and research institutions. Each member of the council will be a physician, scientist or researcher with demonstrated experience in the field of immunology and immunotherapy.
Should the private sector fund this research instead of Prop 38?
Fact: Public funding like Prop 38 is vital to support medical research. More than 99% of new FDA-approved drugs from 2010 to 2019 were built on publicly funded research. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2804378) Prop 38 builds on this proven model by supporting universities and nonprofit researchers to move discoveries from the lab to patients faster and more cost-effectively.
Will the people funding Prop 38 benefit financially?
Fact: Prop 38 is funded by a doctor and philanthropists who will not benefit financially. Only public universities and nonprofit research institutions in California are eligible to receive research funding.
YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocates (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses AssociationCalifornia, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson’s Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, as well as patients, doctors and researchers because it will accelerate life-saving cures. This is a publicly accountable, voter-approved bond.

Prop 38 (2026) Frequently Asked Questions
Updated October 28, 2026
What is Prop 38?
Prop 38 on the 2026 ballot will provide $8.4 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) to advance breakthrough immunology research (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#cures) to develop life-saving cures for the most persistent and debilitating diseases impacting all California families, such as cancer, Alzheimer's and heart disease. This initiative represents real hope and promising cures to help save your life and the life of someone you love.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
Who benefits from Prop 38?
California patients and their families will benefit most from Prop 38. Millions of Californians live with cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, Parkinson's, ALS, diabetes and other serious diseases. Prop 38 will accelerate life-saving immunology research to prevent and cure these diseases, which means more hope and more time together. California patients will also benefit directly with a 20% discount on treatments and cures (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) discovered through Prop 38 funding.
That's why YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy groups (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, Alzheimer's Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses Association\California, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson's Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, alongside patients, doctors and researchers, because it will accelerate life-saving cures.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
What is immunotherapy?
Immunotherapies (https://immunologyexplained.aai.org/) use the body's own immune system to detect and stop diseases. They are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Leading doctors and research scientists are developing immunotherapies that have the potential to prevent and cure a whole range of diseases in our lifetime (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/), including cancer, heart disease, neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, and other diseases such as diabetes, ALS (Lou Gehrig's Disease), HIV/AIDS, muscular dystrophy, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and multiple sclerosis. For the millions of Californians and their loved ones living with these diseases, the life-saving research funded by Prop 38 represents not just hope, but the very real possibility of a cure.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
What diseases and medical conditions would Prop 38 help cure and treat?
Because the immune system plays a role in nearly every aspect of human health, immunology research has the power to prevent, treat and cure a wide range of diseases and conditions – from cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's to Parkinson's, diabetes, ALS, HIV/AIDS, muscular dystrophy, multiple sclerosis, and more. Half of all funds are dedicated specifically to research into cures for Alzheimer's, cancer and heart disease. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm)
Learn more about the power of immunotherapy and how it's already saving lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/).
Copy link for this answer Copied!
Who supports Prop 38?
Prop 38 is supported by a broad and diverse coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates, including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, Alzheimer's Association, ALS Association, American Nurses Association\California, Prostate Cancer Foundation, International Myeloma Foundation, Latino Diabetes Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Blood Cancer United, and Kidney Cancer Association, among many others. Prop 38 is also endorsed by Governor Gavin Newsom (https://yeson38.com/2026/10/09/newsom-endorses-prop-38/), the California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/), the only statewide measure on the 2026 ballot to draw support from both major parties. Together, these organizations advocate for the millions of Californians living with diseases that Prop 38 aims to prevent and cure.

Why is Prop 38 needed now?
Federal funding cuts and uncertainty (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) for California universities and research institutes are delaying medical research, threatening progress toward finding cures. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can't afford to wait. Every funding cut costs patients time, and every research breakthrough gives families more of it.

Where will the research funded by Prop 38 happen?
Medical research funded by Prop 38 will be conducted here in California at leading universities and medical research institutions (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) that are well-qualified to conduct breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research.
That may include University of California campuses, such as UCLA, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, UC San Francisco, UC Irvine, UC Davis, and UC Riverside; private non-profit universities, such as Stanford, USC and Caltech; and non-profit research institutions such as City of Hope, Cedars-Sinai, and Sanford Burnham Prebys, among others.
No bond funds can be awarded to pharmaceutical companies or other for-profit corporations. (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)

Where does the money from Prop 38 go?
Prop 38's innovative network funding model supports California's universities and nonprofit research institutions through equal parts direct funding and investments in new, shared research resources and facilities anchored at a nonprofit institution.
Half of the funds will go to a nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm). This world-class research center will bring together leading scientists, advanced technology, specialized laboratory facilities, patients and clinical trials to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures. This institute will be selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) based on strict accountability requirements.
The other half of funds will be awarded competitively through a grant program to leading universities and nonprofit research institutions across California. This will be overseen by an Advisory Council of leading scientists, doctors and researchers in the field of immunology.
Ultimately, Prop 38 is designed to create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines broad competitive funding with a world-class institution capable of accelerating discoveries into life-saving treatments for patients.

Will Prop 38 make medical treatments more affordable for Californians?
Yes. Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount below the national average (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf). That affordability protection is written directly into the measure — it's not optional.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will also reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.

Yes. Prop 38 funding will only be awarded to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutions (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) with demonstrated expertise in immunology and immunotherapy research. By funding breakthrough research here at home, Prop 38 will support California scientists and universities, create good-paying jobs (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf), and strengthen California's position as a leader in innovative medical research.

How will Prop 38 be paid for?
Prop 38 on the November 2026 ballot is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers (https://yeson38.com/myths-vs-facts/#can-california-afford). Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. Beyond the dollars saved, every cure developed means one less family facing a devastating diagnosis and the financial and emotional burden that comes with it.

01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.

One more question
Why less sunlight for billions in public money?
Despite promises of accountability, the selected institute would not be treated as a public agency under key California transparency and ethics laws, including the Public Records Act, open-meeting requirements and the Political Reform Act.

Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.

Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.

Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.

Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.

Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.

Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.

Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.
