AAI Backs Prop 38: the Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative
4 months ago 2 months ago (https://news.aai.org/2026/06/25/aai-backs-california-immunology-medical-research-cures-initiative/) 2 mins
June 25, 2026
The American Association of Immunologists (AAI), the world’s leading professional organization dedicated to advancing the field of immunology, has announced its support for Proposition 38 (https://caimmunologybond.com/), a historic statewide ballot measure in California that would invest $8.4 billion in cutting-edge immunology research if approved by voters this November.
California is home to some of the nation’s top research institutions, biotechnology companies, and scientific talent. AAI’s support underscores the state’s critical role as a global engine of biomedical innovation—and the importance of sustained investment to maintain that leadership.
“California has long been a U.S. leader in biomedical innovation,” said Loretta Doan, PhD, Chief Executive Officer of AAI. “This initiative represents a forward-looking investment in science, health, and economic growth. By supporting immunology research, California can once again be a shining example to the entire nation as it continues to drive breakthroughs that improve lives and maintains its leadership in developing the next generation of medical advances.”
The immune system plays a central role in nearly all aspects of human health, and advances in immunology have already led to breakthroughs (https://news.aai.org/category/science/)in cancer immunotherapy, vaccines, and treatments for autoimmune diseases—many of which are improving and saving lives today.
AAI joins a growing coalition of scientists, research institutions, patient advocates, and public health leaders supporting the Initiative.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Welcome to the frequently asked questions (FAQs) page of the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM). Here, you’ll find answers to the most common questions you may have on CIRM.
Overview
What is the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM)?
CIRM, was created by the voters of California in 2004 when they overwhelmingly passed Proposition 71 (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/archive/files/about_cirm/prop71.pdf), which authorized $3 billion in funding for stem cell research in California. The agency funds stem cell research at institutions and companies throughout California (as well as institutions and companies outside of the state that conduct a portion of their research in California) with the goal of accelerating treatments to patients with unmet medical needs.
In 2020, California voters approved to continue funding California’s Stem Cell Agency through the passage ofProposition 14: The California Stem Cell Research, Treatments, and Cures Initiative of 2020 (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/sites/default/files/files/about_cirm/Prop-14-full-text.pdf).
What does CIRM do?
CIRM uses money from bond sales to accelerate the pace of cell and gene therapy research in California. CIRM doesn’t carry out research itself. Instead, it solicits research proposals and funds research, training and new facilities throughout the state. A list of all our funded awards is available here (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/grants).
The ultimate goal of our programs is to fast-track stem cell treatments to patients with unmet medical needs. By promoting and encouraging the growth of the stem cell biotechnology sector, the agency is also helping attract the best scientists to the state and establishing California as a global leader in stem cell research.
Why are we paying for stem cell research, shouldn’t that be a job for private industry?
State and national governments have a long history of being involved in the kind of pioneering research that private industry is unable or unwilling to do. Private industry has to focus on the financial return, making them unlikely to fund high-risk projects. Government agencies can fund research with a focus on benefits to the public rather than on making money.
At the Federal level, the government’s support was vital to the success of the Human Genome Project, and funding from the NIH led to the development of 15 of the top 21 drugs introduced between 1965 and 1992.
Private industry tends to focus on projects that are in later stages of development. Without funding for the earliest stages of discovery, there will be no stem cell therapies making it into those later stages where private industry becomes involved.
Scientists have referred to the stage right before industry becomes interested as the “Valley of Death”. It’s an area where promising therapies often languish, because there isn’t enough federal funding to push the projects through to the later stages. CIRM has focused on funding the early research that leads to therapy ideas, and we fund projects that are in the Valley of Death stage, helping to keep good projects on track toward the clinic. We also fund later stages that verify promising therapies and begin clinical trials in people.
Doesn’t the NIH fund stem cell research?
The NIH and other federal agencies do fund stem cell research and do play a vital role in driving scientific discovery. However, they have very broad research interests. With CIRM’s focus on stem cell research, we are able to work closely with academics and industry to craft our funding programs in a way that accelerates the field. Our programs are timed so that researchers with successful projects will have continuous funding from the basic laboratory research through to clinical trials. The NIH tends to focus more heavily on early-stage research, forcing scientists with promising ideas to pause their research and look for new sources of funding as the projects get closer to clinical trials.
CIRM also works closely with our research team partners to help them navigate regulations leading up to clinical trials, and to find industry partners to help fund the later stage research. This ability to focus on accelerating stem cell research toward clinical trials is only possible for an institute with CIRM’s mission.
The NIH is also restricted in the types of research it can fund. Unlike the NIH, CIRM funds the creation of new stem cell lines, lines that have been critical to the success of some research programs.
Patient Access
What is the Alpha Clinics Network?
The Alpha Clinics Network conducts high quality stem cell and gene therapy trials for a wide variety of diseases at leading medical centers in California.
The key to the Network’s success is the ability to accelerate the delivery of treatments to patients through partnerships with patients, medical providers and clinical trial sponsors. These partnerships enable:
Patient-centered clinical trials with the highest standards of care and research
Strategic collaboration with academic and industry teams developing innovative stem and gene cell therapies
Leveraging of resources to promote efficiency, acceleration and increased chances of success
The Network supports both CIRM-funded and non CIRM-funded clinical trials by academic and industry sponsors.
What is the Patient Support Program (PSP)?
The Patient Support Program (PSP) was established to enhance patient access to CIRM-funded clinical trials, an important component of CIRM’s mission and Infrastructure Program.
Through the PSP, CIRM and EVERSANA—a leading provider of global commercial services to the life sciences industry— will address informational, financial and logistical bottlenecks experienced by clinical trial patients and their family members. The PSP will be particularly important for providing equal access to California clinical trial participants.
Services offered by the PSP will include maintaining a Patient Support Center to refer patients to clinical trials, verifying participation and financial support eligibility, as well as administering Patient Assistance Fund (PAF) reimbursements to cover travel expenses, meals, accommodations, childcare, and other out of pocket expenses. Currently, CIRM has been appropriated $15.6 million from the Patient Assistance Fund to support patients.
What is the Community Care Centers for Excellence (CCCE)?
The Community Care Centers of Excellence (CCCE) is a new model for increasing clinical trial access to diverse communities throughout California.
The California Stem Cell Research, Treatments, and Cures Initiative of 2020 (Proposition 14) mandates the establishment of the CCCE Program to promote access across the state to clinical trials, treatments, and therapies arising from CIRM-funded research. The CCCEs are designed to serve as a hub for expanding access to clinical trials, regenerative medicine treatments, and CIRM education and training programs. The program will seek to enlist community-based partnerships to engage populations that can benefit from these treatments.
A strategic aim is to provide equitable access to communities and populations that would otherwise have more limited opportunities in the absence of these centers.
Funding
What has CIRM funded?
The vast majority of our funds go to advance research and the development of new treatments. In support of this goal, we have helped fund the building of much-needed scientific facilities, created innovative initiatives such as the Alpha Clinics Network, and developed educational programs that train future stem cell scientists.
When we were created in 2004, there were few facilities in California where scientists could work with all types of stem cells, particularly embryonic stem cells, and few scientists had access to labs that contained all the equipment needed to do this specialized work. One of our earliest rounds of funding went to build lab spaces that could be shared by researchers within the institution and also used to train younger scientists on how to work with stem cells.
Training was (and is) needed to build the field and create the next generation of stem cell scientists. New therapies won’t happen without people trained to work with stem cells who have both the technical skills and the equipment they need. We have funded programs to train high school students, college students, graduate students and early career scientists. For more about the different educational programs we’ve funded, visit our Education Programs (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/programs/education-and-training/) page.
Most of our funding goes to the research itself. In the early years, because this was such a new field, much of the funding was focused on fundamental, basic science, to help develop a deeper understanding of stem cells and how they worked. More recently we have begun to move the most promising ideas that came out of that earlier funding into clinical trials where they can be tested in people. We’ve also established the Alpha Clinics Network (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/alpha-clinic-network/), the Patient Support Program, and the Community Care Centers for Excellence.
Does CIRM fund clinical trials?
Yes. To date we have funded numerous projects including work in heart disease, cancer, HIV/AIDS, two different forms of blindness and sickle cell disease, to name a few. To learn about the latest list of clinical trials that CIRM is funding, visit our Funding Clinical Trials page (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/clinical-trials/)
Why did CIRM fund new buildings?
When CIRM started in 2004, little research space existed where scientists could work with all types of stem cells, particularly embryonic stem cells, and that contained the equipment needed to work with the cells and – most importantly – develop new therapies. Stem cell scientists were also spread thinly across many research campuses, limiting interactions and slowing the spread of ideas. One of the greatest needs therefore was laboratory space for these scientists to work and collaborate.
The agency provided $271 million toward 12 buildings throughout the state, requiring the institutions to contribute the remaining $543 million to construct and furnish the buildings. That money largely came from donations from individuals or foundations that were inspired by CIRM’s initial commitment to contribute toward the project. This public/private partnership created much-needed work for the construction industry and new, full-time jobs for researchers and other staff.
What organizations are eligible to receive funding?
Funding is open, as it always has been, to both companies and academic institutions.
Applicants do not have to be in California to apply, however, they will have to have some California connection to be eligible for funding. To qualify as a California organization, they must have more than 50% of their employees located in the state, and they must conduct the activities covered by the award in California (with some limited exceptions).

No. Reproductive cloning is specifically prohibited under Proposition 71 and under California law.

Has CIRM made any money for the state?
CIRM’s grants create jobs in California and have expanded the biotechnology industry – propelling California as a world leader in stem cell research. Our grants for new buildings also created construction jobs at a time when the state desperately needed them.

$10.7 billion of additional gross output (sales revenue)
$641.3 million of additional state/local tax revenues
$726.6 million of additional federal tax revenues
56,549 additional full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs, half of which offer salaries considerably higher than the state average

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Welcome to the frequently asked questions (FAQs) page of the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM). Here, you’ll find answers to the most common questions you may have on CIRM.
Overview
What is the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM)?
CIRM, was created by the voters of California in 2004 when they overwhelmingly passed Proposition 71 (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/archive/files/about_cirm/prop71.pdf), which authorized $3 billion in funding for stem cell research in California. The agency funds stem cell research at institutions and companies throughout California (as well as institutions and companies outside of the state that conduct a portion of their research in California) with the goal of accelerating treatments to patients with unmet medical needs.
In 2020, California voters approved to continue funding California’s Stem Cell Agency through the passage ofProposition 14: The California Stem Cell Research, Treatments, and Cures Initiative of 2020 (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/sites/default/files/files/about_cirm/Prop-14-full-text.pdf).
What does CIRM do?
CIRM uses money from bond sales to accelerate the pace of cell and gene therapy research in California. CIRM doesn’t carry out research itself. Instead, it solicits research proposals and funds research, training and new facilities throughout the state. A list of all our funded awards is available here (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/grants).
The ultimate goal of our programs is to fast-track stem cell treatments to patients with unmet medical needs. By promoting and encouraging the growth of the stem cell biotechnology sector, the agency is also helping attract the best scientists to the state and establishing California as a global leader in stem cell research.
Why are we paying for stem cell research, shouldn’t that be a job for private industry?
State and national governments have a long history of being involved in the kind of pioneering research that private industry is unable or unwilling to do. Private industry has to focus on the financial return, making them unlikely to fund high-risk projects. Government agencies can fund research with a focus on benefits to the public rather than on making money.
At the Federal level, the government’s support was vital to the success of the Human Genome Project, and funding from the NIH led to the development of 15 of the top 21 drugs introduced between 1965 and 1992.
Private industry tends to focus on projects that are in later stages of development. Without funding for the earliest stages of discovery, there will be no stem cell therapies making it into those later stages where private industry becomes involved.
Scientists have referred to the stage right before industry becomes interested as the “Valley of Death”. It’s an area where promising therapies often languish, because there isn’t enough federal funding to push the projects through to the later stages. CIRM has focused on funding the early research that leads to therapy ideas, and we fund projects that are in the Valley of Death stage, helping to keep good projects on track toward the clinic. We also fund later stages that verify promising therapies and begin clinical trials in people.
Doesn’t the NIH fund stem cell research?
The NIH and other federal agencies do fund stem cell research and do play a vital role in driving scientific discovery. However, they have very broad research interests. With CIRM’s focus on stem cell research, we are able to work closely with academics and industry to craft our funding programs in a way that accelerates the field. Our programs are timed so that researchers with successful projects will have continuous funding from the basic laboratory research through to clinical trials. The NIH tends to focus more heavily on early-stage research, forcing scientists with promising ideas to pause their research and look for new sources of funding as the projects get closer to clinical trials.
CIRM also works closely with our research team partners to help them navigate regulations leading up to clinical trials, and to find industry partners to help fund the later stage research. This ability to focus on accelerating stem cell research toward clinical trials is only possible for an institute with CIRM’s mission.
The NIH is also restricted in the types of research it can fund. Unlike the NIH, CIRM funds the creation of new stem cell lines, lines that have been critical to the success of some research programs.
Patient Access
What is the Alpha Clinics Network?
The Alpha Clinics Network conducts high quality stem cell and gene therapy trials for a wide variety of diseases at leading medical centers in California.
The key to the Network’s success is the ability to accelerate the delivery of treatments to patients through partnerships with patients, medical providers and clinical trial sponsors. These partnerships enable:
Patient-centered clinical trials with the highest standards of care and research
Strategic collaboration with academic and industry teams developing innovative stem and gene cell therapies
Leveraging of resources to promote efficiency, acceleration and increased chances of success
The Network supports both CIRM-funded and non CIRM-funded clinical trials by academic and industry sponsors.
What is the Patient Support Program (PSP)?
The Patient Support Program (PSP) was established to enhance patient access to CIRM-funded clinical trials, an important component of CIRM’s mission and Infrastructure Program.
Through the PSP, CIRM and EVERSANA—a leading provider of global commercial services to the life sciences industry— will address informational, financial and logistical bottlenecks experienced by clinical trial patients and their family members. The PSP will be particularly important for providing equal access to California clinical trial participants.
Services offered by the PSP will include maintaining a Patient Support Center to refer patients to clinical trials, verifying participation and financial support eligibility, as well as administering Patient Assistance Fund (PAF) reimbursements to cover travel expenses, meals, accommodations, childcare, and other out of pocket expenses. Currently, CIRM has been appropriated $15.6 million from the Patient Assistance Fund to support patients.
What is the Community Care Centers for Excellence (CCCE)?
The Community Care Centers of Excellence (CCCE) is a new model for increasing clinical trial access to diverse communities throughout California.
The California Stem Cell Research, Treatments, and Cures Initiative of 2020 (Proposition 14) mandates the establishment of the CCCE Program to promote access across the state to clinical trials, treatments, and therapies arising from CIRM-funded research. The CCCEs are designed to serve as a hub for expanding access to clinical trials, regenerative medicine treatments, and CIRM education and training programs. The program will seek to enlist community-based partnerships to engage populations that can benefit from these treatments.
A strategic aim is to provide equitable access to communities and populations that would otherwise have more limited opportunities in the absence of these centers.

Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

man cost of delaying this research?
Voting against Prop. 38 would not stop immunology research. California institutions already conduct extensive immunology and immunotherapy research with support from the NIH, philanthropy, industry and other sources.
The financial obligation is certain; the timing and scale of therapeutic benefits are not. Moreover, opportunity costs also have human consequences. For 25 years, debt payments would reduce the resources available for programs that improve health now, including Medi-Cal, vaccination, mental health care, public health preparedness, education and housing. Responsible policy must consider both the potential benefits of new research and the health benefits forgone elsewhere.
The human cost matters on both sides of this decision. Funding tomorrow’s possible cures must be weighed against meeting today’s pressing needs.
Are there other ways the state could incentivize this type of research without taking on general obligation bond debt?
Yes. California could appropriate funds as fiscal conditions permit rather than borrowing the full amount through long-term bonds. It could also establish a statewide biomedical research fund with a broad mission, independent governance, rigorous peer review, public reporting and open competition among qualified institutions. The California Science and Health Research Bond Act introduced in 2026 by Scott Wiener took this approach.
Other options include matching grants that leverage federal or philanthropic support, investments in shared research infrastructure and targeted programs addressing gaps that federal agencies or private markets neglect. These approaches would preserve flexibility, distribute risk and allow priorities to evolve with scientific evidence and public health needs.
“We should fund the best opportunities as science advances, not commit decades of borrowing to one plan and one scientific focus.”
If the state doesn’t fund this research, won’t private pharmaceutical companies just patent the discoveries and charge exorbitant prices?
Public funding does not, by itself, prevent private ownership or high prices. Universities generally license promising discoveries to private companies because product development, large clinical trials, regulatory approval, manufacturing and distribution require resources and capabilities that universities usually do not possess. As a result, even publicly funded discoveries commonly become privately marketed products.
Prop. 38’s discount and revenue-sharing provisions apply only to products arising from research financed by the measure. They do not solve the larger problem of prescription drug pricing. If California wants to address excessive prices, it should do so directly through broadly applicable pharmaceutical purchasing, competition, transparency and affordability policies rather than through an $8.4 billion research bond that is likely to leave the state with excessive debt.
Taxpayers can pay for the research and still struggle to afford the treatment. Public funding alone doesn’t guarantee affordable medicine.
Is the cost of $500 to $600 million a year really that much when compared to the entire state budget?
The 2026-27 California General Fund is approximately $251.5 billion, so annual Prop. 38 debt service would equal about two-tenths of 1% of the General Fund. That percentage may sound small, but $500 million every year for 25 years is not trivial. The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates a total repayment cost of roughly $12 billion.
Nearly 90% of General Fund spending is already committed to education, health and human services, higher education, corrections, debt service and other continuing obligations. The relevant question is therefore not whether California can fit another payment into a very large budget. It is whether this particular commitment is more valuable than the programs, tax relief, reserves or alternative research investments that the same money could support.
Half a billion dollars a year isn’t spare change. It’s a choice about what California can’t fund as a result.
What is your biggest concern with dedicating half the funds to a single research institute?
Our principal concern is that the measure appears to predetermine the recipient of approximately $4.2 billion without naming it or subjecting that allocation to genuine competition. Prop. 38 establishes unusually specific eligibility requirements concerning an institute’s founding date, UC affiliation, affiliated health-system volume, research space and prior philanthropic commitments.
A CalMatters investigation concluded that the criteria very likely leave only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy eligible. UCLA confirmed that it was the only UCLA-affiliated nonprofit meeting the requirements. One of the institute’s billionaire co-founders and principal donors and president of the UCLA Institute Board of Directors, Gary Michelson, is also a major financial backer of Prop. 38.
California has many outstanding public and private research institutions. Allocating billions in public funds to one institute should require an open, transparent and independently judged competition based on scientific merit — not eligibility criteria seemingly tailored to a preselected organization.
Public research dollars should be awarded on scientific merit — not earmarked for a donor’s preferred institution.
Does your opposition stem from the cost of the bond, or the type of research being funded?
Our concerns are both the cost and how research priorities are chosen. Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields, but Prop. 38 would continue the practice of using ballot initiatives to establish scientific priorities. California already has separate voter-created programs for stem-cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused funding structure that is difficult to revise as science and public health needs change.
Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public planning, not campaign advertising. Cancer, Alzheimer’s diseas, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, infectious disease, eye disease, prevention, public health and health services research. Our fiscal concern reinforces the scientific one: California would incur decades of debt for a program that is unusually narrow and insufficiently competitive.
The research is promising. The funding plan is the problem: decades of debt for priorities set by a political campaign instead of scientific competition.
What do proponents of this get most wrong?
Proponents most often blur three distinct questions: whether immunology research is valuable, whether California should support biomedical research and whether Prop. 38 is a sound way to do so. We agree on the first two. We disagree on the third.
The measure concentrates half the money in one apparently preselected institute, restricts all funding to one broad scientific domain and asks taxpayers to accept decades of debt based partly on uncertain future royalties. Supporting science does not require supporting every proposal presented in its name. Good research policy should be competitive, transparent, accountable, adaptable and guided by scientific merit.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
A central question is: Why should scientific priorities be written into the ballot rather than established through an open, expert process? Voters are being asked to approve a highly technical, multibillion-dollar research plan that will be difficult to modify for decades, even as new diseases, technologies and scientific opportunities emerge.
It is also worth asking why the measure does not identify the institute positioned to receive half the funds; why its eligibility criteria are so specific; what other research and public services California will forgo to make the bond payments; and what evidence supports claims that royalties and discounts will provide substantial benefits to taxpayers. Those questions go to the measure’s transparency, fairness and fiscal prudence — not to the value of biomedical science itself.

AAI Backs Prop 38: the Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative
4 months ago 2 months ago (https://news.aai.org/2026/06/25/aai-backs-california-immunology-medical-research-cures-initiative/) 2 mins
June 25, 2026
The American Association of Immunologists (AAI), the world’s leading professional organization dedicated to advancing the field of immunology, has announced its support for Proposition 38 (https://caimmunologybond.com/), a historic statewide ballot measure in California that would invest $8.4 billion in cutting-edge immunology research if approved by voters this November.
California is home to some of the nation’s top research institutions, biotechnology companies, and scientific talent. AAI’s support underscores the state’s critical role as a global engine of biomedical innovation—and the importance of sustained investment to maintain that leadership.
“California has long been a U.S. leader in biomedical innovation,” said Loretta Doan, PhD, Chief Executive Officer of AAI. “This initiative represents a forward-looking investment in science, health, and economic growth. By supporting immunology research, California can once again be a shining example to the entire nation as it continues to drive breakthroughs that improve lives and maintains its leadership in developing the next generation of medical advances.”
The immune system plays a central role in nearly all aspects of human health, and advances in immunology have already led to breakthroughs (https://news.aai.org/category/science/)in cancer immunotherapy, vaccines, and treatments for autoimmune diseases—many of which are improving and saving lives today.
AAI joins a growing coalition of scientists, research institutions, patient advocates, and public health leaders supporting the Initiative.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Welcome to the frequently asked questions (FAQs) page of the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM). Here, you’ll find answers to the most common questions you may have on CIRM.
Overview
What is the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (CIRM)?
CIRM, was created by the voters of California in 2004 when they overwhelmingly passed Proposition 71 (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/archive/files/about_cirm/prop71.pdf), which authorized $3 billion in funding for stem cell research in California. The agency funds stem cell research at institutions and companies throughout California (as well as institutions and companies outside of the state that conduct a portion of their research in California) with the goal of accelerating treatments to patients with unmet medical needs.
In 2020, California voters approved to continue funding California’s Stem Cell Agency through the passage ofProposition 14: The California Stem Cell Research, Treatments, and Cures Initiative of 2020 (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/sites/default/files/files/about_cirm/Prop-14-full-text.pdf).
What does CIRM do?
CIRM uses money from bond sales to accelerate the pace of cell and gene therapy research in California. CIRM doesn’t carry out research itself. Instead, it solicits research proposals and funds research, training and new facilities throughout the state. A list of all our funded awards is available here (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/grants).
The ultimate goal of our programs is to fast-track stem cell treatments to patients with unmet medical needs. By promoting and encouraging the growth of the stem cell biotechnology sector, the agency is also helping attract the best scientists to the state and establishing California as a global leader in stem cell research.
Why are we paying for stem cell research, shouldn’t that be a job for private industry?
State and national governments have a long history of being involved in the kind of pioneering research that private industry is unable or unwilling to do. Private industry has to focus on the financial return, making them unlikely to fund high-risk projects. Government agencies can fund research with a focus on benefits to the public rather than on making money.
At the Federal level, the government’s support was vital to the success of the Human Genome Project, and funding from the NIH led to the development of 15 of the top 21 drugs introduced between 1965 and 1992.
Private industry tends to focus on projects that are in later stages of development. Without funding for the earliest stages of discovery, there will be no stem cell therapies making it into those later stages where private industry becomes involved.
Scientists have referred to the stage right before industry becomes interested as the “Valley of Death”. It’s an area where promising therapies often languish, because there isn’t enough federal funding to push the projects through to the later stages. CIRM has focused on funding the early research that leads to therapy ideas, and we fund projects that are in the Valley of Death stage, helping to keep good projects on track toward the clinic. We also fund later stages that verify promising therapies and begin clinical trials in people.
Doesn’t the NIH fund stem cell research?
The NIH and other federal agencies do fund stem cell research and do play a vital role in driving scientific discovery. However, they have very broad research interests. With CIRM’s focus on stem cell research, we are able to work closely with academics and industry to craft our funding programs in a way that accelerates the field. Our programs are timed so that researchers with successful projects will have continuous funding from the basic laboratory research through to clinical trials. The NIH tends to focus more heavily on early-stage research, forcing scientists with promising ideas to pause their research and look for new sources of funding as the projects get closer to clinical trials.
CIRM also works closely with our research team partners to help them navigate regulations leading up to clinical trials, and to find industry partners to help fund the later stage research. This ability to focus on accelerating stem cell research toward clinical trials is only possible for an institute with CIRM’s mission.
The NIH is also restricted in the types of research it can fund. Unlike the NIH, CIRM funds the creation of new stem cell lines, lines that have been critical to the success of some research programs.
Patient Access
What is the Alpha Clinics Network?
The Alpha Clinics Network conducts high quality stem cell and gene therapy trials for a wide variety of diseases at leading medical centers in California.
The key to the Network’s success is the ability to accelerate the delivery of treatments to patients through partnerships with patients, medical providers and clinical trial sponsors. These partnerships enable:
Patient-centered clinical trials with the highest standards of care and research
Strategic collaboration with academic and industry teams developing innovative stem and gene cell therapies
Leveraging of resources to promote efficiency, acceleration and increased chances of success
The Network supports both CIRM-funded and non CIRM-funded clinical trials by academic and industry sponsors.
What is the Patient Support Program (PSP)?
The Patient Support Program (PSP) was established to enhance patient access to CIRM-funded clinical trials, an important component of CIRM’s mission and Infrastructure Program.
Through the PSP, CIRM and EVERSANA—a leading provider of global commercial services to the life sciences industry— will address informational, financial and logistical bottlenecks experienced by clinical trial patients and their family members. The PSP will be particularly important for providing equal access to California clinical trial participants.
Services offered by the PSP will include maintaining a Patient Support Center to refer patients to clinical trials, verifying participation and financial support eligibility, as well as administering Patient Assistance Fund (PAF) reimbursements to cover travel expenses, meals, accommodations, childcare, and other out of pocket expenses. Currently, CIRM has been appropriated $15.6 million from the Patient Assistance Fund to support patients.
What is the Community Care Centers for Excellence (CCCE)?
The Community Care Centers of Excellence (CCCE) is a new model for increasing clinical trial access to diverse communities throughout California.
The California Stem Cell Research, Treatments, and Cures Initiative of 2020 (Proposition 14) mandates the establishment of the CCCE Program to promote access across the state to clinical trials, treatments, and therapies arising from CIRM-funded research. The CCCEs are designed to serve as a hub for expanding access to clinical trials, regenerative medicine treatments, and CIRM education and training programs. The program will seek to enlist community-based partnerships to engage populations that can benefit from these treatments.
A strategic aim is to provide equitable access to communities and populations that would otherwise have more limited opportunities in the absence of these centers.
Funding
What has CIRM funded?
The vast majority of our funds go to advance research and the development of new treatments. In support of this goal, we have helped fund the building of much-needed scientific facilities, created innovative initiatives such as the Alpha Clinics Network, and developed educational programs that train future stem cell scientists.
When we were created in 2004, there were few facilities in California where scientists could work with all types of stem cells, particularly embryonic stem cells, and few scientists had access to labs that contained all the equipment needed to do this specialized work. One of our earliest rounds of funding went to build lab spaces that could be shared by researchers within the institution and also used to train younger scientists on how to work with stem cells.
Training was (and is) needed to build the field and create the next generation of stem cell scientists. New therapies won’t happen without people trained to work with stem cells who have both the technical skills and the equipment they need. We have funded programs to train high school students, college students, graduate students and early career scientists. For more about the different educational programs we’ve funded, visit our Education Programs (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/programs/education-and-training/) page.
Most of our funding goes to the research itself. In the early years, because this was such a new field, much of the funding was focused on fundamental, basic science, to help develop a deeper understanding of stem cells and how they worked. More recently we have begun to move the most promising ideas that came out of that earlier funding into clinical trials where they can be tested in people. We’ve also established the Alpha Clinics Network (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/alpha-clinic-network/), the Patient Support Program, and the Community Care Centers for Excellence.
Does CIRM fund clinical trials?
Yes. To date we have funded numerous projects including work in heart disease, cancer, HIV/AIDS, two different forms of blindness and sickle cell disease, to name a few. To learn about the latest list of clinical trials that CIRM is funding, visit our Funding Clinical Trials page (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/clinical-trials/)
Why did CIRM fund new buildings?
When CIRM started in 2004, little research space existed where scientists could work with all types of stem cells, particularly embryonic stem cells, and that contained the equipment needed to work with the cells and – most importantly – develop new therapies. Stem cell scientists were also spread thinly across many research campuses, limiting interactions and slowing the spread of ideas. One of the greatest needs therefore was laboratory space for these scientists to work and collaborate.
The agency provided $271 million toward 12 buildings throughout the state, requiring the institutions to contribute the remaining $543 million to construct and furnish the buildings. That money largely came from donations from individuals or foundations that were inspired by CIRM’s initial commitment to contribute toward the project. This public/private partnership created much-needed work for the construction industry and new, full-time jobs for researchers and other staff.
What organizations are eligible to receive funding?
Funding is open, as it always has been, to both companies and academic institutions.
Applicants do not have to be in California to apply, however, they will have to have some California connection to be eligible for funding. To qualify as a California organization, they must have more than 50% of their employees located in the state, and they must conduct the activities covered by the award in California (with some limited exceptions).
Can the funding be used to fund research on human reproductive cloning?
No. Reproductive cloning is specifically prohibited under Proposition 71 and under California law.
Economic Impact
Has CIRM made any money for the state?
CIRM’s grants create jobs in California and have expanded the biotechnology industry – propelling California as a world leader in stem cell research. Our grants for new buildings also created construction jobs at a time when the state desperately needed them.
A 2019 independent Economic Impact Report (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/sites/default/files/files/about_cirm/CIRM_Economic%20Impact%20Report_10_3_19%20v.2.pdf) conducted by the Schaeffer Center for Health Policy and Economics at USC says that CIRM has had a major impact on California’s economy, creating tens of thousands of new jobs, generating hundreds of millions of dollars in new taxes, and producing billions of dollars in additional revenue for the state. The report looked at the impacts of CIRM funding on both the state and national economy from the start of the Stem Cell Agency in 2004 to the end of 2018.
The estimated impacts from the report are:
$10.7 billion of additional gross output (sales revenue)
$641.3 million of additional state/local tax revenues
$726.6 million of additional federal tax revenues
56,549 additional full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs, half of which offer salaries considerably higher than the state average
You can read the press release announcing the 2019 Economic Impact Report here (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/about-cirm/newsroom/press-releases/10092019-new-report-says-stem-cell-agency-produces-measurable-0/) and additional reports from previous years on our Publications page (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/webinars-and-workshops/).
As our funding begins to lead to the development of new therapies, a portion of the profits from the sale of those therapies will also be returned to the state. And of course because these therapies are treating diseases that currently have no effective remedy we will also be reducing the health care burden on California, reducing medical spending and improving the quality of life for people in the state.
Resources
How can I stay up to date about CIRM’s activities?
We have several ways of keeping people up to date on our research progress.
Sign up for our email lists (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/sign-up-for-updates/). We have four different lists that provide people with information about CIRM news, new funding opportunities, and opportunities to attend public meetings.
Read our blog, The Stem Cellar (http://blog.cirm.ca.gov/). We report on progress by CIRM grantees and update readers on the field of stem cell research.
Follow us on social media. We have active Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/CaliforniaInstituteforRegenerativeMedicine/), Instagram (https://www.instagram.com/CIRMnews/), Twitter/X (https://twitter.com/cirmnews), and YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/user/CIRMTV) channels.
Can I donate to CIRM?
Under Proposition 71, CIRM can accept donations of “additional revenue and real and personal property (including cash), including, but not limited to gifts, royalties, interest, and appropriations that may be used to supplement annual research grant funding and the operations of the institute.” To implement this section, our governing board has adopted a policy and procedure on the acceptance of donated real and personal property.

Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.
