Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.
This story was originally published October 8, 2026 at 5:00 AM .

**Weighing research funding arguments**

I'm thinking about verifying the budget for federal cuts and how it relates to the perceived value of research. It’s essential to be thorough. For supporting arguments, global immunology research shows social benefits, and basic research is underfunded. There’s potential for public funds to yield great returns. Additionally, controlling overhead and ensuring transparency are key points. Major patient groups also support this choice, so it seems there’s a strong case for continuing investments in research.**Analyzing funding support**

It looks like both major parties are backing this initiative, which seems fiscally responsible. The support from notable scientists adds credibility, but it’s important to remember that this isn’t the only factor in determining merit. Coordinating advanced facilities could really help reduce costs and barriers in clinical research. However, there are concerns about misrepresentations regarding revenue guarantees and the need for significant funding to achieve returns. The discussion surrounding the 2028 proposals also raises questions about funding timelines.**Evaluating research strategy**

I’m considering that the existing information doesn't fully address competitive aspects. I think adding one more batch of academic budgets and primary agreements could be useful. A bit of additional time, maybe around 8 minutes, wouldn't hurt the user. It looks like the tool doesn't indicate any real latency, and we've been at this for about 15 minutes now. 

We might continue with just 4 sources, ensuring it's concise while targeting essential reports, especially around LAO deficits.

***2026‑27 Budget Problem Now Larger Than Anticipated.*** Under our revenue and spending estimates, the Legislature faces an almost $18 billion budget problem in 2026‑27.
### Executive Summary
This is about $5 billion larger than the budget problem anticipated by the administration in June, despite improvements in revenue.
This is because constitutional spending requirements under Proposition 98 (1988) and Proposition 2 (2014) almost entirely offset revenue gains.
Moreover, we estimate costs in other programs to be about $6 billion higher than anticipated.
Starting in 2027‑28, we estimate structural deficits to grow to about $35 billion annually due to spending growth continuing to outstrip revenue growth.

#### $18 Billion Budget Problem in 2026‑27

In addition, the administration estimated the state would continue to face structural deficits between $15 billion and $25 billion through 2028‑29.

# Overview of the Spending Plan
## General Fund Condition
### Budget Window
Figure 3 summarizes the condition of the General Fund under the revenue and spending assumptions in the June 2026 budget package, as estimated by the administration.
Under these projections, the state ends 2026‑27 with $4.5 billion in the SFEU.
(The SFEU is the state’s operating reserve and essentially functions like an end‑of‑year balance.)
The revised balance of $29.2 billion in the SFEU for 2025‑26 reflects, in large part, a significant upward revision to 2025‑26 revenues.
That revenue upgrade leaves the budget close to structurally balanced in that year but does not carry through to 2026‑27, as the administration assumes revenues are essentially flat in 2026‑27.
As a result, drawing down that elevated 2025‑26 balance—along with other choices described earlier in this report—allows the state to cover costs in 2026‑27 that would not otherwise be covered by that year’s revenues on their own.
In other words, the state has a structural imbalance in 2026‑27, even though the enacted budget is balanced.

Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters In summary The Trump administration cancelled $2 billion of research grants to University of California professors. Their legal team says it has proof that those terminations were unconstitutional. Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State. Federal agencies that terminated more than a thousand research grants at the University of California last year admitted that they used keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy and COVID-19 to screen for projects that ran afoul of the Trump administration’s priorities. It’s an admission that lawyers for the research professors say is proof (https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.450653/gov.uscourts.cand.450653.210.0_2.pdf) that the agencies illegally cancelled nearly $2 billion in grants. And that’s a major development in a lawsuit filed by UC researchers against the Trump administration to permanently get their grants back. The researchers’ legal team is now asking the judge in the case to skip a trial and formally declare that the White House repeatedly violated the constitution, including the First Amendment. A court hearing on whether that’ll happen is scheduled for Oct. 20. The federal agencies made the admission about the keywords in signed stipulations filed in federal court last week in a case called Thakur v. Trump that’s been ongoing since last spring (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2025/06/health-research-california/#:~:text=UC%20researchers%20may%20get%20science%2C%20environmental%20grants%20back). READ NEXT He spent decades researching dementia. Trump’s DEI purge killed his grant, and dozens more (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2025/04/health-research/) April 10, 2025 April 10, 2025 The stipulations in the court filing show the agencies “did not terminate any grants based on alleged noncompliance with the terms of the grant” and instead used “general criteria, rather than grant-specific assessment of each award’s compliance, or performance,” the lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote. Lawyers for the UC professors now contend that the admission proves three wide-ranging constitutional violations: By using keyword searches to review hundreds of grants and terminate them en masse rather than reviewing them individually on their merits, the Trump administration targeted research it found politically disfavorable, which is a First Amendment violation. In terminating 283 Department of Energy grants from states where a majority voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, and leaving untouched hundreds of grants that went to “red” states, the Trump administration wrongly punished researchers for merely living in states the White House politically opposed. And by terminating billions of dollars in grants, and never rerouting that money to other grant opportunities, the Trump administration violated the constitution by not spending money in ways Congress specifically required through laws it passed on how research funds should be used. CalMatters emailed the U.S. Department of Justice, which acts as the legal defense for the federal agencies, on July 16 to ask whether it agrees that the federal grant-making agency stipulations mean the Trump administration violated the constitutional rights of researchers. A spokesperson for the Justice Department didn’t respond by publication time. History of lawsuit The judge in this case, Rita F. Lin, has repeatedly sided with the UC professors and issued several preliminary injunctions forcing the federal agencies to restore the grants while she reviews the full merits of the case. This includes the restoration of hundreds of grants at UCLA that the Trump administration sought to suspend over its allegations (https://calmatters.org/education/2025/09/ucla-research-grants/#:~:text=What%20the%20Trump%20administration%20has%20argued) that the university tolerated antisemitism and permitted transgender women to compete on women’s sports teams. Those allegations were also the subject (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2025/11/uc/) of a demand from the White House for UCLA to pay $1.2 billion or experience an additional cascade of research freezes. However, months before Trump sought that settlement UCLA took steps to address antisemitism on campus, including commissioning a task force to recommend ways to create a more welcoming environment for Jewish students. Lin, a Biden appointee, faulted the administration for disregarding those efforts by UCLA in a preliminary injunction for a different but related lawsuit. The Trump administration’s justification for terminating the grants did not “mention the remedial steps UCLA had already taken to address the issues described,” Lin wrote. Lawyers for professors in the Thakur case now want Lin to make a final ruling ordering the grants to be restored, rather than a preliminary one. Even if that were to happen, the federal agencies could decide to appeal Lin’s ruling to a higher court. The stakes “are huge,” lawyers for the professors in the Thakur case wrote. If the White House is “allowed to terminate this funding, the researchers, graduate students, and program staff that relied on the grants to pursue their lives’ work will all suffer significant damage to their reputations and careers.” The lawyers warn of lifesaving cures that will never be developed, new understandings of diseases that will go unexplored, and the decline in the country’s global standing as an international juggernaut in publicly funded research. Sign up for free Δ Using keywords to target disfavored grants The agencies admitted to using keywords in various ways, according to a CalMatters review of the new court filings. The Department of Transportation identified (https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.450653/gov.uscourts.cand.450653.211.2_1.pdf) six grants for projects worth about $42 million to terminate because they sought “transportation equity,” prioritized “disadvantaged communities,” or focused on “diversifying the transportation workforce” and “equity.” The termination of three of those grants led by a UC Davis professor resulted in 77 researchers abandoning 79 in-progress projects. Lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote that the project leaders were also forced to lay off or scramble to replace funding for more than 40 graduate and undergraduate research assistants. The National Institutes of Health admitted to using an internal search tool to flag UC grants that mentioned “health equity,” “work force diversity,” “structural racism,” and “sexual orientation.” The NIH alone suspended or cancelled more than 1,000 UC grants, including nearly 700 at UCLA, related to vaccines, cancer research and disparities in health outcomes. That figure is newly disclosed in a court filing — last year, UCLA indicated that closer to 500 NIH grants were terminated. The health research agency also declared that it’s possible that DOGE, the short-lived (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/07/07/doge-shuts-down-elon-musk/90836161007/) federal office that billionaire Elon Musk led in 2025, used AI to target grants for termination. Lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote to the judge that these admissions show the agencies “identified the viewpoints they wanted to suppress, searched the grants they funded for those that expressed those viewpoints, and terminated those grants on that basis.” That violates the researchers’ First Amendment rights, the lawyers wrote. The Environmental Protection Agency, one of the named agencies in the suit, is in the process of settling (https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.450653/gov.uscourts.cand.450653.209.0.pdf) with lawyers for the UC professors to avoid further litigation. A separate federal district judge in Massachusetts last week dealt the Trump administration a blow (https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mad.286247/gov.uscourts.mad.286247.122.0_2.pdf) in its ability to terminate grants and withhold federal funding. The White House relied on a legal phrase in many of its funding cancellations — “no longer effectuates . . . agency priorities.” California and 22 other states sued, arguing that there’s no law or right for the federal government to cancel funding based on new program goals and White House desires after the grants were already awarded. The judge agreed. also in driving the U.S. economy. For every $1 invested in NIH research,

About this data: UMR’s annual economic calculations assume that the research funding awarded each fiscal year works its way into the economy in that same year. However, as this report
notes, the NIH made substantially increased use of multi-year funding in FY2025, whereby it obligates the full amount of the award in the year it was funded rather than only the amount for
that year. According to calculations by the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC), approximately 7% of total grant funding in FY2025 was to multi-year funded awards compared
to 5% in FY2024. UMR’s calculations for FY2025 do not attempt to separate out the multi-year-funded grants from those funded in the traditional manner. As in past years, the calculations
assume all funding was spent in the fiscal year.
The analysis for this report was performed by Ronald Horst, Ph.D., Inforum. Calculation of the jobs and economic activity resulting from NIH research awards in each state relies heavily on the
Regional Input-Output Modeling System (RIMS) parameters maintained by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). BEA updates the RIMS parameters annually, although the economic data
used lags by two years. Additionally, BEA does a major, “benchmark,” revision to RIMS parameters every five years. UMR’s data for FY2025 was calculated in January 2026 using the most
recently published RIMS parameters at that time, which rely on economic data for calendar year 2023. The data shown here for years FY2016-FY2024 were calculated using earlier versions
of BEA’s RIMS parameters or approximations for those years. Given the way the RIMS parameters change over time, the data presented here should be viewed as a series of snapshots of the
economic effects of NIH funding in each year.

The Impact of
Multi-Year Funding
There were significant disruptions to NIH research funding in 2025,
including delays in reviewing and making awards. As of mid-June,
research funds awarded by the NIH were about 30% below prior-year
levels.1 Yet, by the end of the fiscal year, the NIH had made up this
shortfall and met the September 30 deadline to spend its budget.
To do this, the NIH made significant use of a budget mechanism
called multi-year funding whereby it obligated the full amount of
a multi-year grant in the year it was awarded (2025) rather than in
annual increments. While this enabled the agency to spend its budget
quickly, it also resulted in a substantial reduction in total awards
funded. This is because the funds allocated for the remaining years
of the multi-year funding awards were set aside and reserved, making
them unavailable for other new awards. In FY2025, 5,564 fewer
grants were funded than in FY2024.

2026 UPDATE | NIH’S ROLE IN SUSTAINING THE U.S. ECONOMY | 7
Drop in NIH
Funding Rates
A concern with the NIH’s increased use of multi-
year funding is that it reduces the amount of
money available to fund promising research and
researchers. In fact, NIH funding rates — a measure
of how many researchers seeking support were
successful — dropped to about 17% in FY2025.2
This is the lowest level in nearly 30 years and
compares to 26% in 2024 and 30% in 2023.3
Nineteen states and the District of Columbia
saw at least a 10% decrease in the number of
awards received in FY2025 compared to the
previous year.
Given congressional appropriators’ “strong
concern” about the negative impact of multi-year
funding on research application success rates and
the resulting reduction in the number of grants
NIH can fund, the final FY2026 Labor, Health and
Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies
funding bill includes specific language limiting
NIH’s future use of the funding strategy.4

Background
Founded by visionary philanthropists Dr. Gary Michelson, Dr. Eric Esrailian, Dr. Arie Belldegrun, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken and Sean Parker, the CIII was formally established as a public-private partnership with the State of California. (Governor Newsom Announces World-Leading Science & Technology Research Center in Los Angeles (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/)). The CIII will be operated as an independent medical research organization, with faculty affiliated with the renowned David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA.
Also home to UCLA Center for Quantum Science and Engineering (https://www.cqse.ucla.edu/index.html), UCLA Research Park will be the world’s first facility to bring together immunology, quantum computing, and AI, together with translational research and product development capacity, biotech incubator and accelerator space. As an economic engine for Southern California, CIII will rapidly become the world's epicenter for innovation for immunologically-based health solutions.
Next Steps
Building on its momentum, CIII is:
Developing its initial five year strategic plan (2025-2029)
Recruiting senior scientific and executive leadership
Identifying and securing philanthropic and industrial partners
Planning, designing and building the research facilities at UCLA Research Park
Establishing its governing board, scientific, and other advisory committees
By creating a unique culture of convergent biological and computer sciences entrepreneurial research and industrial partnerships, laser focused on harnessing the power of the human immune system, the CIII offers the potential to rapidly discover and develop new technologies and products to prevent, treat and cure humanity’s most intractable diseases.

### Your guide to Proposition 38: Immunology and immunotherapy research funding
The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
